content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
This paper proposes applying an attention mechanism to the input of a recurrent neural network such that the resulting architecture can learn to store only parts of the input which are actually relevant to predicting the future. This is motivated by the concept of a d-separating set, which serves as a sufficient set of observed variables to predict the influence of hidden variables. The idea is implemented as a soft spatial attention mechanism applied to the output of a CNN before it is input to an RNN. The architecture also includes a feedforward component to which the attention mechanism is not applied. The benefits of this architecture are explored in a simple but illustrative traffic domain where the light at an intersection is controlled using only local information. The architecture is also explored on several Atari games as well as a variant of pong which randomly hides certain observations to increase partial observability.

The motivation of learning d-separating sets so that the agent can focus on only the variables that can have a meaningful impact on the future is interesting and perhaps warrants further exploration. However, I find the method presented in this paper to be lacking in significant novelty or new insight and recommend rejection primarily for that reason. The method itself is only very loosely connected to the idea of d-separation sets as ultimately the whole thing is just trained by standard back-prop and there is no direct exploitation or learning of a graph structure. The method seems to me to be essentially a rebranding of spatial attention, the benefits of which are fairly well explored, but applied only to the recurrent part of the architecture which I don't consider enough of a contribution to publish at this venue.

In addition to this, the experiments provide limited insight or evidence of the effectiveness of the architecture. While the traffic example is reasonable, the Atari games tested (aside from perhaps flickering pong) have only fairly trivial partial observability (e.g. the direction an object is travelling cannot be determined from a single frame). This makes them a fairly poor domain for testing the proposed approach and does not seem in line with the proposed motivation of the paper.

Also, according to the appendix default hyper-parameters were used for everything except the additional parameters of InfluenceNet, which were hand-tuned, further limiting the significance of the experiments. In particular, I have trouble believing the RNN baseline couldn't be made to do well on flickering pong given a more favourable hyper-parameter setting. Also, was the recurrent architecture tested a regular RNN or a more sophisticated architecture like a GRU or LSTM? Given I would think one of that latter would be a more relevant baseline, as well as a more relevant setting to apply the proposed method, given ordinary RNNs are rarely used in practice.

While I don't feel the paper presented here is ready for publication, the idea of studying of how we can isolate sufficient variables for representing the history is worthwhile and I hope the authors continue expanding on this direction.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #3 (part 2)
content.comment:
(5) ‘I have trouble believing the RNN baseline couldn't be made to do well on flickering pong given a more favourable hyper-parameter setting’

This concern was also raised by reviewer #2 who found an implementation of A3C+LSTM that seems to perform better. Please refer to the response there.

(6) ‘was the recurrent architecture tested a regular RNN or a more sophisticated architecture like a GRU or LSTM?’

Both the InfluenceNet model and the RNN baseline implement an LSTM network. We wanted to emphasize that the InfluenceNet model does not require any recurrent architecture in particular, but will clarify that both our implementations (InfluenceNet and RNN) use LSTMs in the new version of the paper.

(7) ‘the idea of studying of how we can isolate sufficient variables for representing the history is worthwhile’

We are encouraged by the fact that you agree that the core objective that we address in this paper (learning which variables we need to remember about, to deal with non-Markovianess of a subset of variables) is worthwhile. We hope that our rebuttal has taken away the main concern on novelty, and clarified the other questions. Thank you again for your detailed comments.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #3 (part 1)
content.comment:
Thank you very much for your critical but thorough review. We very much appreciate the time you took to review our work. Please find the responses to your concerns below:

(1) ‘The method itself is only very loosely connected to the idea of d-separation sets as ultimately the whole thing is just trained by standard back-prop and there is no direct exploitation or learning of a graph structure.’

In the manual version of the method, our knowledge about the d-separating variables is directly encoded in the network by selecting the regions (the d-patches) that form the boundary to the hidden state variables (see Figure 4 left). As such, there is a direct connection to d-separating sets (irrespective of whether the computational graph is optimized via back-prop). The inductive bias created by limiting what variables we remember about leads to very good results in the traffic control task (see the orange curve in Figure 4 right).

However, not in all applications, it is easy to manually select the d-patches. Also, the relevant d-patches could depend on the state itself. Therefore, we aim to automatically select the d-patches (by means of an attention mechanism). Although it is true that the mechanism is trained using backpropagation, if we impose a constraint on the amount of information that is fed into the RNN, the algorithm should learn to put more weight on those regions of the memory input that influence the agent’s future transitions and rewards the most. Our experiments in Section 5.3 and Appendix B confirm this hypothesis. The network learns to consistently select the important regions that need to be memorized.

(2) ‘The method seems to me to be essentially a rebranding of spatial attention, the benefits of which are fairly well explored’

As of this date, we are only aware of one other work that applies spatial attention to RL in a similar fashion, which is the cited paper by Sorokin et al, (2015).  However, as we explain in the related work section, their method is missing the FNN component. This means that their model can not benefit from our observation that many variables are (approximately) Markov, while only a small subset needs to be treated as non-Markovian (by feeding the d-patches needed for their prediction into an RNN). We believe this is the reason for the poor performance they obtain in some of the Atari games. In other words, while the model learns to select the regions containing the most relevant information it also discards important information. In the case of Breakout for instance, the agent can track the ball but it doesn’t know the layout of the bricks and the location of the paddle which are quite relevant for estimating value. The fact that we do not need to memorize certain variables because they are conditionally independent of the hidden ones does not mean that they are not useful in inferring the underlying state of the MDP.

If there are other papers where spatial attention has been used to restrict the input to the agent’s internal memory, we kindly ask you to provide the specific pointers or retract the claim of lack of novelty or new insight.

(3) ‘the Atari games tested (aside from perhaps flickering pong) have only fairly trivial partial observability (e.g. the direction an object is travelling cannot be determined from a single frame). This makes them a fairly poor domain for testing the proposed approach and does not seem in line with the proposed motivation of the paper.’

The Atari games have become a popular benchmark to test POMDP Deep RL methods (Hausknecht & Stone 2015, Sorokin 2015). In fact, even in these domains where stacking multiple frames remains a practical and effective solution, InfluenceNet can reach the same level of performance as the FNN model. That is to say, we don’t see this as a weakness but a strength. Of course, the benefits are more obvious in environments with long-term dependencies (traffic control and flickering pong) and in these InfluenceNet does show a clear advantage over the baseline.  Besides, in the Atari environments, manual specification of the d-patches is not possible, which makes them great candidates to motivate and test the automatic d-patch selection mechanism.

(4) ‘According to the appendix default hyper-parameters were used for everything except the additional parameters of InfluenceNet, which were hand-tuned, further limiting the significance of the experiments’

We used the same hyperparameter configuration reported by Schulman (2017), which was optimized specifically for the Atari games. We believe that the fact that we could not properly optimize the additional parameters of InfluenceNet (due to the lack of resources) is only a disadvantage for our method but in no case should it affect the performance of the baselines.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper considers the RL problem of learning an agent's policy in a high dimensional and only partially observable environment that can be modelled as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). The authors propose InfluenceNet, a model-free deep RL architecture. The main intuition is that in a POMDP the Markov property is not satisfied, but on the basis of influence-based abstraction the non-Markovian dependencies can be accounted for by conditioning on the history of a subset of the locally observable variables. InfluenceNet incorporates this idea by processing the current local observation separately with (1) a FNN and (2) a weighted linear combination of vectors representing particular regions in the input image with an RNN. The weighting of the linear combination in (2) is determined by an attention mechanism and the results of (1) and (2) are combined to determine value and action probabilities. Experimental results on a simple traffic control task and different Atari games support the effectiveness of the approach in determining the regions which contain relevant information. Further, the results indicate that (while improving the runtime performance) InfluenceNets performance is on par or even better in comparison to two simple baseline setups for problems in which the information can be reduced to a small subset of the input.

Overall, the paper is marginally below the acceptance threshold, but I am willing to increase my score if some more clarification are provided and the results of the experiments are revisited and extended (see comments below). 

The paper provides a methodological contribution by an extension of existing approaches from the field of POMDP methods and the application of an attention mechanism to address the problem of high dimensional input which I believe can be quite useful for the RL community. The submission is well written and easy to follow, the problem is well motivated and the concept of separating the Markovian and non-Markovian dependencies in the proposed architecture is explained in a reasonable way. Suitable experimental results support the architectual decisions and illustrate the benefits of the proposed method, but should be revisited with respect to the given remarks below. The paper includes reasonably complete information that will help to reproduce them and I think that the reproducibility of the results is good, even though I did not explicitly validate it. The authors provide the source code whose documentation could be improved (README, empty folder etc.).


Questions / clarifications / remarks:

The experiments should consider an architecture based on an LSTM in addition to the RNN as baseline for a recurrent network. Hausknecht & Stone (2015) and Sorokin et al. (2015), which are both cited in the paper, use LSTMs in their architectures and can be seen as related approaches and the current state of research for the problem at hand. The influence of the long-term memory component of an LSTM would be particularly interesting when considering the memory capability of an agent.

The results for Pong and flickering Pong with the RNN look suspiciously poor as if the agent would behave totally at random. The results should be double checked and if they are correct, please comment on them. Again, an approach based on a LSTM should be considered here, as it is known to work better than random on the problem of Pong. Check for example https://www.endtoend.ai/envs/gym/atari/pong/ and "A3C LSTM".

Furthermore, it should be worked out where the increase in performance of InfluenceNet comes from compared to completely recurrent models. How much can be attributed to the separate FNN added to the architecture and how much to the attention mechanism?

Table 1 shows the runtime performance of the individual methods. It is not clear how the d-patches were selected for InfluenceNet. Since it can be assumed that there are differences in runtime performance between a manual and automatic selection of d-patches, both variants should be listed.


Minor comments:

Page 2:     - typo: R(s_t, a_t) is defines the ... >> R(s_t, a_t) defines the ...
Page 8:     - typo: InlfuenceNet >> InfluenceNet
Figure 2:   - The shape and color of action a_C is not explained and does not correspond to the shape of action a_A; missing arrow from x_2 to the other state factors for t=3
Figure 4:   - blank space in the second last sentence
Table 1:    - One result for the Atari games is incorrectly highlighted bold 
Table 2:    - Multiple results are highlighted as being the best 


Final remark:

The paper shows a very high agreement with the following (workshop) paper and should be considered as plagiarism if the authors do not match:
Miguel Suau de Castro, Elena Congeduti, Rolf A.N. Starre, Aleksander Czechowski, and Frans A. Oliehoek. Influence-Based Abstraction in Deep Reinforcement Learning. In Proceedings of the AAMAS Workshop on Adaptive Learning Agents (ALA), May 2019.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #2
content.comment:
Thank you for your very thoughtful review and insightful comments. We very much appreciate the time you took to review our work. Please find the responses to the points raised below:

(1) ‘The experiments should consider an architecture based on an LSTM in addition to the RNN as baseline for a recurrent network.’

Both the InfluenceNet model and the RNN baseline implement an LSTM network. We wanted to emphasize that the InfluenceNet model does not require any recurrent architecture in particular, but we will clarify that both our implementations (InfluenceNet and RNN) use LSTMs in the new version of the paper.

(2) ‘The results for Pong and flickering Pong with the RNN look suspiciously poor as if the agent would behave totally at random’

We are aware of this discrepancy and have been trying to find the reason ever since the results came out. The way we process the observations that are received from the environment is the same as in the OpenAI baselines. We are also quite certain the RNN model is correctly implemented (it works well in all the other environments we tested). We use the same hyperparameters reported by Schulman et al. (2017) for PPO and Hausknecht & Stone (2015) for the recurrent component. The best explanation we can give is that the PPO algorithm is driving the model towards a local minimum in this particular environment. Note that we are using PPO and not A3C and that there are no published results of PPO+LSTM for Pong.

Most importantly, we would like to point out that even if we were able to match the results of Mnih et al. (2015), yielding a value of 10.7 after 4 days of training on 16 CPUs, this still would not affect our claim of superiority: InfluenceNet was trained to a performance of 20.80 in 50 h on 8 CPUs.

(3) ‘it should be worked out where the increase in performance of InfluenceNet comes from compared to completely recurrent models. How much can be attributed to the separate FNN added to the architecture and how much to the attention mechanism’

If this refers to evaluating a model that combines an FNN and a full RNN. We believe that the full RNN can be considered a generalization of the FNN+RNN model. Besides, the RNN model is already computationally very expensive to train, adding the FNN block would only make it slower. Nonetheless, we agree that testing this configuration can be worthwhile and hope to have some results before the end of the discussion period. 

If, on the other hand, this comment refers to comparing the automatic d-patch selection (attention) with the manual version.  This is already shown for the traffic control task in Figure 4.

(4) ‘It is not clear how the d-patches were selected for InfluenceNet’

The manual d-patches used in the traffic scenario are depicted in Figure 4. We chose the regions in the image that correspond to the outgoing lanes since these clearly contain the d-separating variables.

(5) ‘Since it can be assumed that there are differences in runtime performance between a manual and automatic selection of d-patches, both variants should be listed.’

The reported values correspond to the automatic version which is slightly slower than the manual version due to the computing overhead caused by the additional weights of the automatic d-patch selection mechanism. We will list the runtimes of the manual version in the new revision.

(6) Minor comments:

We will fix all the mentioned typos in the new version. As for the tables, multiple values are highlighted when the differences are not statistically significant. This will be clarified in the Table caption.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper proposes a method called InfluenceNet to deal with partial observations in reinforcement learning. The idea is to keep track of only a small amount of available information using a recurrent mechanism and attention - based on the previous work of Oliehoek et al (2012). The model is composed a RNN (tracking the past) and a FNN (current only) which jointly influence the value and policy functions. The model is tested on a simple traffic control task and four Atari video games.

It is hard to distill novelty out of the paper and it is unclear how the idea of "influence-based abstraction" helps in the evaluated cases, where the performance of the InfluenceNet is highly correlated with the FNN component. At best the proposed is a simple combination of FNN and RNN, and the RNN hardly does any job. The experiments are very inadequate to empirically confirm any hypotheses.

The reference list seems to ignore much of recent works in solving partial observations, e.g., memory-based methods.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #1
content.comment:
Thank you for your review. Find our responses to your concerns below:
	
(1)‘It is hard to distill novelty out of the paper’

The novelty and contribution are quite explicitly indicated at the bottom of page 1:

'Here we show how to adapt this approach to high dimensional reinforcement learning (RL) problems where no explicit model of the world is available.  In particular, we use the insights from IBA to propose a different way of organizing the recurrent neural network [...]'

Also, see the summary in the conclusions ('In this paper, we investigated if ideas from influence-based abstraction can be adapted to complex RL problems [...]').

We point out that Reviewer #2 gave a very good summary of our contributions.

(2) ‘it is unclear how the idea of "influence-based abstraction” helps in the evaluated cases, where the performance of the InfluenceNet is highly correlated with the FNN component. At best the proposed is a simple combination of FNN and RNN, and the RNN hardly does any job’

Let us clarify what we believe is a misconception:  The FNN component of InfluenceNet only takes a single observation (frame) while the FNN baseline uses a history of observations (multiple stacked frames) to remove partial observability.  Feeding only the most recent frame in the Atari games leads to very poor performance in all the 4 Atari games. This also occurs in the traffic example where neither using a single frame nor stacking multiple ones helps due to long-term dependencies. 

Our experiments show that even by feeding a single frame and storing in memory only the relevant areas of the input, we get substantially better rewards (-5 vs -10 in traffic and 20 vs 16.08 in flickering pong) and/or computational speed-ups at roughly the same performance than the FNN baseline, which stacks more than one frame (see Table 2). These benefits are even more obvious when comparing InfluenceNet against the RNN baseline.

(3) ‘The experiments are very inadequate to empirically confirm any hypotheses.’

This strikes us as unmotivated and incorrect criticism as we will explain next.

As stated at the beginning of the experiments section: Our first hypothesis is that InfluenceNet improves over full recurrent models, which are fed with the entire input image. Secondly, we wanted to show that our method represents a better choice for handling partial observability than using a fixed-sized window of past frames. 

The results of the experiments support these two hypotheses: InfluenceNet obtains better performance in terms of reward and compute time than the RNN and FNN (with frame stacking) baselines. The results indicate that, by feeding into the recurrent cells only the relevant variables, we reduce training times and facilitate the learning process, offering a better alternative than ordinary recurrent architectures. As for the second hypothesis, we show that while the InflfuenceNet model can hold long-term memories, stacking multiple frames rapidly becomes impractical as the need for memorizing events in the distant past increases (traffic control and flickering pong).

We also tested the automatic d-patch selection mechanism. In section 5.3 we show that the d-patch selection mechanism can capture the regions of the input image that contain the d-separating variables. In section 5.4 we show that the selected information is sufficient to estimate the future influence of the hidden state variables.

Having said this, we kindly ask the reviewer to suggest what other experiments could be conducted to validate the above hypotheses and improve our work.


(4) ‘The reference list seems to ignore much of recent works in solving partial observations, e.g., memory-based methods.’

We are happy to include citations to relevant papers that we have missed but would expect a review that makes a critical statement about ignoring related work, to include the actual pointers to papers that we should have cited.
